I'm 83 years old and I've been working this land for 60 years. My bones ache in the winter now, and there's only me and my wife left at home — our children have gone to the cities. With only 5 mu of land, I can't afford to waste a single fen, but I also know I can't push myself like I used to. I've seen good years and bad years in Quzhou, and I trust what my eyes and hands tell me more than any book.

For the winter wheat, I'll plant the whole 5 mu. I'll use an improved seed variety — not the most expensive hybrid, but the one I've saved and selected from good ears over the years, mixed with some bags I bought from the county supply store that my neighbors also use. The soil here is decent but tired, so I need to give it some food. I'll spread about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu, 7 kg of phosphorus, and 5 kg of potassium. I have the well, so I'll irrigate three times: once after sowing to help germination and overwintering, once at green-up in spring, and once at the grain-filling stage. I'll spray pesticide twice — once for aphids in spring and once for fungal diseases before heading. I'll do rotary tillage before sowing; my neighbor has a small machine and he'll help me. I expect about 500 kg per mu if the spring rain cooperates.

For summer maize, right after the wheat harvest in early June, I'll plant maize on the same 5 mu. I'll use hybrid seed — everyone here does, and it gives better ears. For fertilizer, I'll put down about 18 kg nitrogen per mu, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium. I'll irrigate twice because summer rains sometimes come and sometimes don't, and maize is thirsty at tasseling and grain filling. Two pesticide sprays should handle the corn borers and leaf blights. I won't do deep tillage for the maize — there's no time between wheat harvest and maize sowing, and my old rotary tiller works fine for a light pass. I hope for around 550 kg per mu.

I keep my inputs modest because at my age, carrying heavy fertilizer bags is hard, and my wife and I need to save a little for medicine and food. But I've farmed this land long enough to know its moods.
